Mr 0 T. Grantham, manager of the Imperial Cotton Company, Hamilton, sends us the following "etter from their New York selling agents, which may be found of interest as illustrating the difficulties which Canadian manufacturers are meeting with in endeavouring to market their goods in Japan :
New York, April 22, 1905.
Dear Sir,-I regret having to report that in spite of continued efforts, we have found it lm-

possible to sell any of the Canadian goods for export to Japan. During the past six or eight months we hare sold very large blocks of goods manufactured in the United States for export to that market, but, in spite of our best efforts, and of offers, of price concessions, we have not been able to ship a yard of your goods to Japan.
Knowing that your goods were equal in every respect to the American made duck, we were forced to look for some other reasons for the discrimination against the Canadian goods. We found, in the first place, that there was a preferential of five per cent, in favour of the duty on American duck. In order to offset that, we offered the Canadian goods at five per cent less than the American goods, so that they might go in through the customs on the same basis. Even at this price concession, we were unable to effect any sales, in spite of the fact that the Japanese were most desirous of obtaining goods promptly, and were thoroughly scouring the American markets for goods which could be delivered at au early date. We then found out that the reason we could not effect sales was not so much on account of the prices of goods as because there was a sentimental prejudice in Japanese official circles against Canadian-made goods. It seems that the Japanese feel that they were discriminated against by the Canadian government, and that the Canadian government was not willing, at some time in the past, to make the same arrangements with Japan as with the United States and England.
I believe that it is more on account of this prejudice than for any other reason, that we cannot effect the sale of your goods in this mar-+ *7 an<^ ^ ^ *s *n an5r way possible for you to bring about more friendly relations between your government and the Japanese officials, we believe that it will materially help the trade of the Dominion.
Yours very truly,
J. SPENiCER TURNER COMPANY.

Some four or five weeks ago I notified the Minister of Militia that I purposed bringing up during the course of the session the purchase of a site for a militia camp at Kentvilie, N.S., and he then explained that he was familiar with all the details of the case and that it could he explained. In justice to the Minister of Militia the House and the country I think it is proper that we should have an explanation, the best possible he can give. The statement as furnished to me contains the following data :	It shows that the government expropriated about 640 acres of land for the purposes of a camp ground, I believe, at or near the village of Kentvilie, N.S. That land was previously owned by a number of people, but before the expropriation proceedings it was purchased by Messrs. II. P. Dodge, and H. H. Wickwire, members of the local legislature of the province of Nova Scotia, staunch Liberals and members of King's county. I have here a statement which shows how a number of these lands were purchased, contained in a newspaper published in the locality, and I may as well show the manner in which these lands were acquired. For instance one was purchased from John Redden, et al trustees. &c.. by 'Milliard II. Fulton, barrister. Halifax, Race Track, Kentvilie 26 acres, May 30, 1002, for $1,250. Then there was a transference of the same property from W. H. Fulton and his wife to H. H. Wickwire, barrister,

I do not know that I have anything more to say, except this : There was an evident intention or desire in some way to show, by quoting an extract from a speech I made in this House some time ago, that I had mis-stated the facts in that case; that while I had stated in the House that not $1,000 had been spent on militia buildings for the militia of my county since I have been minister, enormous sums had been spent-amounting to $20,000 or $25,000-in constructing rifle ranges. And the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sam. Hughes) even showed that some $1,200 or $1,300 had been spent in improving an old drill hall in that county. Now, I am prepared to admit that, to the extent of the difference between $1.000 and $1,200 or $1,300, I was in error in saying that only $1,000 had been spent in militia buildings in my county for the use of the corps immediately concerned, the corps having their headquarters in my county. The evident intention-the unfair intention on the part of the hon. gentleman was to show that my statement was not true and that thousands and tens of

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext:
thousands had been spent in my county for the militia of my county, when the hon. gentleman knew perfectly well, quite as well as he will after I have told him again, that all this expenditure, except the paltry $1,200 I have referred to, was expended for the whole militia of Nova Scotia. This expenditure was for the establishment of a rifle range, one of sixteen targets and one of the best rifle ranges in Canada, and securing a camp ground of CIO acres-a mile square-for the use of the militia not only of the whole province of Nova Scotia, but of part of that of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick as well. I have the satisfaction of knowing, from the highest military authorities in this Dominion, that the camp ground at Kentville is one of the best if not the best in the Dominion of Canada to-day.
But the hon. gentleman tries in some round-about way to cast suspicion of wrong doing upon this transaction. Where is the wrong doing ? It was not for me to say and I am not saying whether the land was worth one dollar, or ten dollars, or twenty dollars, that is none of my business. The value of the land has been submitted to the proper court to ascertain and it will be ascertained. It is the duty of the judge to get the best evidence with respect to the value of the land. I may say, however, Mr. Speaker, that this camp Is situated within a mile of the shire town of my county, the important town of Kentville. This 040 acres of land are well situated, surrounded by orchards on every side, with a railway passing along the whole of one side.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I have just made an inquiry by telephone to the officers of the Exchequer Court as to the position, which was not very clear. I found that the claim was referred to Mr; Crawley for inquiry and report. Mr. Crawley took evidence and reported in favour of the claimants, fixing the value of the land at $38,400. The Crown appealed, and the judge sent back the case to Mr. Crawley for further inquiry and report. That is the situation of the matter at present.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext:
As I said, it is sub judice, it is open to change. It is the duty of the judge to make up his opinion ns to the value of the land, and I do not think it can be in safer hands than in the hands of Mr. Justice Burbidge, where I am sure the interest of the public as well as the interest of the owner of the land will receive every due and fair consideration. Now what more is there to be said ? That is the whole story, it seems to me. The value is to be fixed, the land has been expropriated, everything is above board. The records are there to show. I have not familiarized myself particularly witli what has been done. I only know that the greatest care was taken to assure that the inter-

est of the people of this country might he served.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: The minister did not seem to deal with that part of the statement that $35,000 had been spent on the rifle range, and that the contract had been exceeded by $6,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: There is not a word of truth in that statement. I am glad my hon. friend has called my attention to it, because I agree with him that it requires an answer. The intention to construct the rifle range on these grounds was published in the newspapers in Halifax, and I think in the newspapers in this city, so that it was open to all the people of Canada to tender, and the lowest tenderer got the work, an Ottawa firm. There were several tenders, but the people who got the work are men who have done a great deal of work of this kind, are experts in the matter. They constructed the rifle Tange in Ottawa, they constructed the rifle range in Montreal and at Three Rivers, they have constructed many rifle ranges throughout Canada, and in every case they have received the contract only after open competition, and after due advertising in the public press. That is the way they got the tender at Kentville. I do not know whether one kind of wood was substituted for another or not, but I do know that the engineers in my department are exceedingly careful in all such matters, that the most careful inspection is insisted upon ; and if any change or substitution took place, it only took place under the authority of the chief engineer of the Militia Department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: As to the appropriation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: There is an annual vote of $75,000 for the construction of rifle ranges, and as I understand it the $19,000-1 think this range cost $19,600, possibly $20,000-was taken out of that vote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: The contract price has been adhered to ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Absolutely. When the estimates come down there will be a further opportunity to discuss this matter, and if any additional information is required I will be glad to give it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I think, before these estimates come down and are taken up again, the minister might, in justice to the House, lay on the table whatever papers in connection with the matter are in his possession.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I shall be very glad to do so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I would not like to say anything more about it until I see these papers. I will say this much, however, that I would like to get $38,400 for 640 acres of land in that part of Nova Scotia.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I do not know whether $38,400 will be paid for it or not. But I can tell my hon. friend that he will find in that part of Nova Scotia, which I think he has visited, lots of land, farming, lands and orchard lands, which he could not buy for $600 an acre.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: The hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Sam. Hughes) read from the local papers some comments with reference to this land. The minister says, and no doubt it is quite true, that this subject attracted a great deal of attention during the last election in his riding. I do not wonder that it did. Why, two local members of parliament, by inspiration I presume, had gone around the country and bought land at $2 an acre, and in a very short time afterwards found they could sell it for $60. This must' have been pretty exceptional land, with all due deference to the county, and the minister does not contradict it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I did not think it was necessary for me to go into that. I have no idea what they paid. All I know as to the value of the land is this, that some thirty years ago about twenty-five acres of land which was made a hunting park, which is a part of this range, was purchased in the native condition, you might say, for $25 and acre. I ascertained that fact, and that is all I know about it. But I feel quite confident that a fair valuation for that land would be anywhere between $20 and $30.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Well, it seems that that part of it which is the race track they sold at a fairly good price. But whatever prompted the two local members to go and buy 60 acres of land at $2 an acre, must have been a question that suggested itself to the electors of that riding.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: And they answered it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows how they answered thfe question up in Edmonton a few weeks ago on the school question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: No doubt of it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: And they will answer the same question later on in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Don't forget Quebec.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman may set that off against Centre Toronto. But be that as it may, not only do we find these two inspired local members buying 60 acres of land, but, upon inspiration that came from Ottawa, they go back and buy 200 acres more at $1 an acre, then there is another batch of it picked up at $10 an acre. The result is that as soon as it changes hands it advances from $1 and $2



an acre to rbout $60 an acre. We do not know and we have no intimation here as to who this Mr. Crawley is, or how Mr. Crawley came to be appointed. We have no intimation here as to how the case was conducted on behalf of the Crown, and it will seem as strange to the country as it was to the electors there. Perhaps the hon. minister may enlighten us why it is that these local members should go and pick up 300 or 400 acres of land which they could buy at $1 and $2 an acre and which had lain there useless for years and that suddenly an intimation is given to these gentlemen that this land is to be used for a large militia camp ground. The hon. minister states that this is a desirable tract of land, being surrounded by magnificent orchards. It must have been the irony of fate that there -should have been beautiful orchards around a tract of land that went begging at $1 an acre. It must have been struck by lightning.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: You ought to go down there and see it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I might have seen it for a long time if it could be purchased at from $1 to $2 an acre. It strikes me that it is a fair matter for discussion and I think the hon. minister should endeavour to let us know what made these gentlemen wake up so suddenly and buy this waste land at $1 and $2 an acre that immediately advances to $60 an acre. Perhaps an inkling was given to these gentlemen in the same way as it was given to certain gentlemen in regard to the half-breed scrip in the Northwest. It seems that there was an Order in Council passed that was never made public until months afterwards, and when it was made public there was nothing left. The senators and1 members from the Northwest interested had picked up all the scrip that was going begging. I hope the question will be renewed again when the estimates are under discussion, and that the hon. minister will enlighten us as to why these local members were permitted to pick up this land*at $1 and $2 an acre and to sell it afterwards at $60 an acre.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Has it yet been established that it is worth $60 au acre ? Why does my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) assume that the government agreed to pay $60 an acre for it ? The matter is still before the courts, and if the land was purchased recently for $1 or $2 an acre is it not a reasonable assumption that that fact will be investigated by the judge of the Exchequer Court, and that whatever weight is entitled to be attached to that argument by the court will be given to the transaction by Judge Burbidge ? Would that not be a more reasonable assumption rather than to take it for granted that Judge Burbidge is going to authorize the payment of $60 an acre for that which was purchased for from

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: $1 to $2 an acre ? If it is a fact that the property was purchased recently for $1 or $2 an acre, that fact undoubtedly would be investigated by Judge Burbidge and it would have whatever weight it was entitled to in fixing the value of the land.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Would Mr. Justice Burbidge, having referred this matter to this gentleman in Nova Scotia, Mr. Crawley, be in a position to know if this land had been purchased for this price, if it had not been represented to him here in this manner ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: It is the business of Mr. Justice Burbidge to know all these things. That is the purpose for which he holds his court. In regard to Mr. Crawley, I know nothing of his relations with this transaction, but I know that Mr. Crawley is a most respected barrister in Nova Scotia, a son of the late Rev. Dr. Crawley, a man whose name is honoured throughout Nova Scotia, and I have no hesitation in saying that I would have the fullest confidence in the perfect fairness of any transaction with which Mr. Crawley is connected.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext:
It would seem that some person must have confidence in Mr. Crawley and as Mr. Crawley has made his report Judge Burbidge will have to deal with exactly the same evidence when it comes before him. If Mr. Crawley's judgment is good, I do not assume it is going to be appealed against. Perhaps the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) will recollect a very remarkable case in Quebec. I refer to the case at Levis. This was a most extraordinary case. Perhaps the case with which we are now dealing may outrival it but it is hardly possible that it could do so. The Levis case was one in which the Intercolonial Railway desired to acquire a lot of land. The then Minister of Railways and Canals, Mr. Blair, sent down one of his trusted agents. He went around and saw the proprietors and they were all ready to sell at $1 a foot. When he made his report what happened ? The minister, Mr. Blair, initialled the report and recommended the purchase of the land. Mr. Archer, a barrister of Montreal, and a partner of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefoutaine) and Mr. Pugsley, were retained by some of the parties and what happened after that ? The price was advanced from $1 a foot to $2.50 a foot. Then came a letter from the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) advising Mr. Blair to accept a figure 300 per cent more than had been originally offered by the parties who owned the land and that was backed up- this is all on record in ' Hansard '

by the statement that the Prime Minister has recommended that the deal should be made on this basis. Then there was an appeal to the Exchequer Court with the result that the augmented price was allowed. I think that experience has taught us that these appeals have not resulted in the country

getting cheap property in the long run.
I know nothing about the merits of this case, but I do remember the Levis case in which, as a result of the interference of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, this land doubled and trebled in value.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I do not know what happened . in the case of the St. Charles branch expropriation ; I am not familiar with that case in which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) says that Judge Burbidge increased the value of land 300 per cent. But, there is one fact that is very patent to the House. It is that according to the Exchequer Court Act the judge has the right *to refer any case to an arbitrator, or a referee if it pleases him. I appeared on the Exchequer Court in Quebec representing the Crown in a certain claim of Mr. H. M. Price of Quebec in which the court referred the case to the registrar, Mr. Au-dette. A report is made on the facts by the registrar, or referee and then the judge is free to accept or reject that report. He applies the law to the facts. It has happened not once, not twice, but in hundreds of cases in which reports were made by a referee or arbitrator or registrar that the judge would not accept his report. He would reverse the report. It happened in one case in which my firm was interested siine months ago in the matter of Paul vs. the King. The report of the referee was in favour of our clients, but when it came before the court it was reversed. It happens every day. The judge is entitled under the Exchequer Court Act to refer a case to a referee or arbitrator. Therefore, there is nothing very surprising in this case in the fact that it was referred to an arbitrator in the province of Nova Scotia. The judge is not bound by the report which is made by the arbitrator or referee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Is not the judge bound by the evidence taken by the referee? I ask that question because of a remark made by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). The hon. Minister of Finance said that it was the judge's business to get the evidence and to find these things out. Is it not a fact that the judge will take no evidence except such as is brought before the referee where the investigation is made?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: If the judge is not there himself the registrar is there. The registrar acts for the judge in fifty cases out of a hundred usually. The court is there, the court controls the case, and my hon. friend, I am sure, would not say that Mr. Justice Burbidge would accept only one-sided evidence in that case.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext:
I am not suggesting anything of the kind. I merely want to see that we understand each other.
212i

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that the court is always represented by the registrar.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I want to find out whether the judge had before him such evidence as was reported by this referee. The judge does not hear original evidence ; he simply goes on evidence taken by the referee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: The judge decides, not on one-sided evidence, but on full evidence. The court is conducted on legal lines. There has been no complaint on that score.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: It is quite open to the judge of the Exchequer Count, when he proceeds on the report of Mr. Crawley or any other person, to order further evidence if he is not satisfied with the evidence before him. He is in no sense bound, as my hon. friend would intimate, by the report of Mr. Crawley. He may order either a new reference or a hearing of evidence before himself as Exchequer Court judge ; or, after hearing this evidence, he may order a new hearing, he may set aside Mr. Crawley's report entirely. So long as the case is not decided by the judge himself, it is open to further evidence.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend the Solicitor General know whether any decision was rendered in the Exchequer Court in the case referred to by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) ; and if so, what figure was fixed by the court for the indemnity ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I am not aware that any amount was fixed by the Exchequer Court. I understood from my hon. friend that it was not referred to the Exchequer Court, but that the amount was fixed by the department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Perhaps the Minister of Railways would be informed on that point- what the expropriation at Ldvis cost per foot.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I am not familiar with it. It was some time before I was in the department, and I do not know the facts. I have heard of that, as I have heard of the St. Charles branch case.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I would ask the Minister of Militia to (be good enough to bring down and lay on the table as soon as convenient the data in this matter. I may say that I do not propose waiting to take it up on the militia estimates. I find that the militia estimates are passed on some evening, conveniently, when certain gentlemen happen to be out of the House. The estimates are then quietly slipped through.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows that an item was reserved in the estimates.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I know. That is also held to the end of the session, and passed through in the same way. I would like the hon. gentleman to bring down the name of the owner of these 640 acres that were purchased for a drill ground, the cost of the ground, the award of the commission, the nature of the timber used in the butts, whether c-edar or hemlock-he can get a report from his engineer on this .point. I do not think I have laid myself open to the charge of being unfair. However, I will not discuss that, as I shall have another opportunity of doing so. I want the report of Mr. Crawiley to the Exchequer Court judge brought down.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: How can I get the report ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext:
I am notifying the government, and the toon. Minister of Militia is a member of it.
Sir FRBDERlCK BORDEN. If my hon. -friend will allow me, it seems to me that every object will be served when this case is completed. I have no doubt that the judgment will be given in a short time, and I shall be glad to lay the judgment, the evidence and all the papers connected with the case on the table of the House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: The minister will see that when the judgment is delivered that will end it. Maybe we can throw a little light on the matter to help the judgment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I think the Minister of Militia, instead of feeling hurt at this matter being brought up, if he has the interest of the country at heart, should be glad that we are strengthening the hands of Judge Burbidge and helping him to get this collateral evidence. I trust that the minister will have all this information brought down at an early date.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I will bring down such papers as I can get. I have not any idea of the owners of the land, except from what I have read in the newspapers and what the hon. gentleman has said. Any papers in the department bearing on this matter I shall be giad to bring down at the earliest possible moment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: We are not discussing this question from any other standpoint than that of the public interest, at the present time at least. The minister has heard today that that land, that was bought for $1 an acre, was sold to the government through the medium of interested parties, who no doubt got information that it was to be taken for such a purpose, or would be likely to be taken, and were therefore quite willing to go into the speculation. Neither of these gentlemen would have bought one arpent of that sand land unless he expected to turn it over in a speculation. Now that 1 the minister has heard of this immense bill,

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: which must have astounded himself, of $38,400 for this land, on the report of the referee, based on evidence obtained by one of the most able and hot one of the scrupulous lawyers in the province of Nova Scotia, against a young man, not the ablest or the strongest, on the part of the Crown, he must see that it looks like a plant. I am not saying that it is, but it looks like it. The minister says that he cannot get at the value of the land. He can easily ascertain from whom Messrs. Dodge and Wicliwire got this land, for he can get at the record of the transfer ; there is a way by which the evidence of those who sold the land in the first place can be got, if they did not give it in the Crawley inquest; and if it transpires that that land was bought at $1 an acre by these people, not for their own use, but in order to palm it off on the government for $38,400, I do not care a penny if the case went through a thousand exchequer courts, it is a transaction that should be sat upon. If anything ever smelt like a plant, this does ; and the minister will not do his duty unless he finds out what that land cost these go-betweens ; and if it turns out that they got it for $1 an acre, it is the duty of the government not to pay that money if there is any power in the universe to prevent them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend. That is what the Exchequer Court was created for, and I would assume that, with the ease left to be dealt with by that court, the public interest would be looked after. I assume that evidence was brought forward as to the proper price to pay for the land.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: The Exchequer Court has nothing to do with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Oh, yes ; the Exchequer Court has the right to inquire for further evidence.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: [DOT] The Exchequer Court does not initiate the procuring of evidence. That is left to the parties-the Crown on the one hand and the claimants on the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Perhaps it is not a material point, but Mr. Justice Burbidge is himself a native of King's county, and would have enough knowledge of the value of land around there to enable him to make due inquiries.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Mr. Justice Burbidge does not take the evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: He can.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: He simply appoints the referee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: At .his discretion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext:
That will be the evidence taken by the referee. Who brings the evidence, who engineers it ? Dodge &

Wdckwire. Through whom ? Through a vorv able lawyer, to say the least of it, who defends the case for the government. Mr. Tremaine, of Mellreith & Tremaine. Now the evidence is so engineered, it is so made to appear to Mr. Crawley by some means or other, they may be fair or they mav not, that he gives a judgment that the' land is worth so much.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: He does not give a judgment but an award.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: It is an opinion which is equivalent to a judgment. That comes before the Court of Exchequer and Judge Burbidge may have as much personal knowledge as he pleases about that land but he is bound to take the award of Mr. *Crawley.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.

I never saw him do it. My knowledge of the practice of the Exchequer Court is this : that the judge of the Exchequer Court, like every other judge in every other court I have heard of, leaves the conduct of the case to the counsel on each side. If he has taken a new course it is within the last two years, at least so far as cases from the province of .Nova Scotia are concerned. I have been Mr. STOCKTON.
engaged in a good many cases and never knew him to do anything else. If counsel for the Crown declined to cross-examine witnesses brought by the claimant the judge of the Exchequer Court would not say a word. If counsel for the Crown declined to produce any evidence in contradiction to that brought by the claimant, the judge would have nothing to say, and if the counsel for the Crown made no objection when counsel for the claimant made motion for a judgment, the judge of the Exchequer Court would, so far as my experience goes, confirm the report.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: The judge has acted differently to my knowledge and the law is there permitting him to ignore the report.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: That is not the point. My hon. friend does not seem to be able to understand the point. When counsel for the Crown raises objection there is a most ample power for the judge; every one knows that. But the Solicitor General says that the judge of the Exchequer Court is in the habit of practically taking the case out of the hands of counsel for the Crown and doing their duty himself.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I am not saying that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: It must be because he has learned a certain distrust of these counsel for the Crown that he has taken this course. He never did it in my experience certainly. He always supposes that counsel know more about their own eases than he does and leaves it to them to shape their case as they see fit. He leaves it to them to argue the case as they see fit, just as the judges in every court do. The judges do not raise objections which are not put forward by counsel on behalf of their own clients. To do so would be to take the case out of the hands of the counsel ; and most counsel, if they found a judge undertaking a course, which my hon. friend says is now the universal practice in the Exchequer Court, would simply take off their gowns and retire from the conduct of the case. I should certainly do so if the judge of any court undertook to conduct my case for me and to raise objections on behalf of my client that I did not propose to raise. It seems to me most unusual, yet I am bound to accept my hon. friend's statement that not only has it occurred in his practice but it is the almost universal practice.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I shall state the ease again, as my hon. friend appears to believe I do not understand the question. I say that many times a judge may not sit personally in a case but appoint a referee.

The referee will make a report and the judge is not bound by that report. Mr. R. L. BORDEN. The hon. gentleman went a great deal further. BORDEN. I never saw' it done. Mr. LEMIEUX. It happens every day in the Exchequer Court. Mr. LENNOX. The position taken by the hon. the Solicitor General in very extraordinary. There are a good many lawyers in this House, and I think he has stated a position new to almost every and perhaps to every law'yer in the House. The position he takes is that the judge of the Ex-chquer Court is not the judge but really the counsel, and the counsel. I understand, on behalf of the Crown. The Minister of Militia took the position, in the first instance. and it was followed up by the Solicitor General and the lion.- member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt), that of his own motion and without any suggestion from counsel the judge of the Exchequer Court would take the matter into his own hands and practically say to the counsel: You sit down. I am going to conduct this case. Well, although I am not a lawyer of prominence, I would not put up with any such treatment from any judge. I know that in some instances a judge will undertake to ask a question or two but very rarely indeed; but to say that in fifty cases out a hundred a judge will take the" matter in his own hands is a very poor compliment indeed to the counsel acting for the Crown and a very poor compliment to the government who engage such counsel. It is well the people should know-assuming that the Solicitor General is correct-the kind of baby counsel which the Crown must have engaged cases before the Exchequer Court, because no counsel of sufficient ability to conduct an important case before the Exchequer Court would put up with that kind of treatment. Mr. LEMIEUX. Let me point out to the hon. gentleman the last line of section 98 : The judge may, in his discretion, decline to act on the evidence. Mr. STOCKTON. That is not what we are discussing. In the ordinary course o1 his duties, the judge has that discretion under the Act, but he would only use it oi a suggestion from the Crown counsel, ant the position taken by the Solicitor Genera to-dav is that the judge of the Exchequei Court is the counsel for the governmenl	and not the judge as between the Crown and the subject to see that fair compensation is given for property taken. Well, let me say that the judge is not the counsel. He is there to hold the scales evenly betwen the Crown and the subject. The counsel on either side present the case as they think best, and the judge adjudicates on the case as presented. Mr. LANCASTER. The Solicitor General will find almost the same words in any statute defining the powers of a judge. Certainly the Court of Appeal may in its discretion grant a new trial, but It does not act on that discretion without an application from counsel. Mr. LEMIEUX. The Exchequer Court has very exceptional power. You would not find the same in any court, but it is to be found in the statute governing the Exchequer Court. Mr. SAM. HUGHES. Would the Minister of Finance be good enough to obtain the evidence in connection with this report of the referee and have it laid on the table ? Mr. FIELDING. Mr. FIELDING. I shall call the attention of the Minister of Justice to the statement made. I can offer no opinion. All I can say is that I shall call his attention to the matter. - Mr. FOSTER. That is all my hon. friend can do. maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: For a number of years we have had an officer of the archives branch in Paris picking out documents bearing on Canadian history. These are to be copied. But the force who have been copying these documents have not been able to copy nearly as many as have been picked out. The result is that, while documents have been discovered bearing upon our history- and copies of which we ought to have-to a number sufficient to fill about 3,000 volumes, we have actually copied and on the shelves here only about 300 volumes. The archivist has asked that we should proceed more rapidly with this work and this we have been doing for the last few months. An additional amount is required for this work. Moreover the archivist has been trying to prepare an indexed catalogue of the works of his branch. There has never been a complete reference book of the papers and documents. For the work of preparing such a catalogue Mr. Hrey has been engaged. I found it neces-salary to pay him $75 a month, which the Auditor General says is not consistent with the Civil Service Act.

speechtext: I received a letter a short time ago from the Holstein breeders. I have not the letter at hand at the moment, but as I recollect it, they seemed to think that too much respect had been paid to the freight handlers' side of the question. The minister will probably know to what I am alluding and will be able to explain it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I think I can explain it. Probably my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) has received the same representations which have been made to myself. I do not think the difficulty he mentions is exactly the one which is most dwelt upon bv the Holstein breeders. In assembling the records so that the Department of Agriculture at Ottawa might be able to affix the official stamp to the pedigree certificates, I found, on investigation, that it was absolutely necessary, as a practical matter, that the keeping of the records should be conducted here and not at other points in the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: That is it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: The Holstein breeders have desired to keep, their records still at a place called St. George, in Western Ontario. I have had to say to them that I did not see how it was practically possible for us to affix the stamp of the department to these records, and examine them in the way we ought to do before affixing that stamp, unless the records were kept here. All the other record associations have agreed to transfer their records here. I have made that a part of the conditions on which the official stamp could be affixed, and I have informed the Holstein breeders that I am ready to do in their case what I have done in the case of other breeders, but I cannot see how I can make them an exception, when I have made this condition a sine qua non with the other associations.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext:
That would seem fair at first glance. But are there no exceptional circumstances in the position of the breeders of Holsteins ? I understand they have hitherto kept their records at St. George.
I suppose they have an office there and that all breeders of Holsteins send in their pedigrees to that office ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Then, I take it their objection is that they would be put to expense by establishing an office here ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Then what is it ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.

I do not know what it is.
I have been given various reasons for it, but the Holstein breeders have given no reason except that they desired to keep their records at St. George. Other breeders' associations have transferred their records from the places where they were formerly kept. More of them were kept in Toronto, and these have been transferred to Ottawa. Some records were kept in Nova Scotia and some in New Brunswick, and these have been transferred here. There are some in Quebec which 1 hope will be transferred here within a few weeks or months, some who have made objection. But they all agree without, exception that it is in the interest of the whole work that the records should be transferred here. The Holstein people are the only ones that have yet held out any objection.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: How many associations will transfer their records here ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I think about a dozen.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I understand the minister will expend $5,000 altogether, and $3,000 now. Would he tell us how this money is to be expended?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I must premise that explanation by one or two statements. The nationalization of the records is for the purpose of combining all the records so that there shall be only one herd book for any one breed. There have been in some cases several herd books.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: The statutes said only one association.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext:
The Dominion statute said there should be only one national association, but there have been several local ones. For instance, in the province of Quebec there is a herd book in which various kinds of cattle, sheep and swine are all registered. Each individual breed has been registered in Toronto, called The Dominion Swine Breeder's Records. But in the province of Quebec, Yorkshire swine and Berkshire swine have been registered. Now the object of the nationalization of the records is to do away with all these, so that there may be only one national record. For that purpose we have got to assemble here the various records that have been in existence. We find that with those records are certain books and documents which it is necessary to have here for the proper carrying on in future of this work. When an application comes in for registration, we have to refer to the books to see whether the pedigree is right for registration. I have had to make financial arrangements with some of these smaller herd books for the purpose of getting their books made up. For instance, I have had to pay to the Nova Scotia Department of Agriculture, $300 in consideration of which they have agreed to send all their books and documents up here.
I have made an arrangement with Mr. Henry Wade, of Toronto, for a number of books which are his private property, not the property of the Breeders' Association but which are very necessary to have for my officers here to carry on this work in the department. I have had to pay $500 for those books. I have had to make an arrangement with the New Brunswick government and pay them $600 for what they have. I expect to have to make an arrangement with the Quebec breeders for some of their records, I do not know how much I shall have to pay. Besides that, we will have to purchase a considerable number of record books. For instance, we will have to procure volumes of shorthorn records in England, we will have to have in some cases certain record books in the United States, so as to be able to refer back when an application comes in ; we have to buy these books. The record associations themselves have books many of which we will have to obtain for the purpose of the department. It is for these purposes that this money is needed. We have already made arrangements which involve an expenditure of nearly $2,000. and I expect before the 1st of July to have to expend another $1,000. The rest of this money I will not expend until after the 1st of July. I hope $5,000 will cover our needs, but I am not sure of it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: The $5,000 are the initial expenses to put it on a working basis ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Yes. I hope that will do, but that does not mean for the expenses of. the current year. That will come in under the vote for the live stock division, which I will ask parliament to grant in a short time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: That will be granted from year to year to keep it going.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: That will be part of a large vote which I ask parliament for my live stock association.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I would like the minister to state about what he thinks the actual expense will be of the change that was made by the recent Act, that is, to keep this national register in operation once it is assembled here at Ottawa.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: I think it will cost about $3,000 a year in the future.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: Who gets the fee ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PURCHASE OF MILITIA CAMP AT KENTV1LLE, N.S.
speechtext: That fee goes to the Breeders' Association, we have nothing to do with it. The agreement which this association signed with me specifies distinctly that I shall have nothing whatever to do with their finances, because those are the finances of the individual breeders' associations. I may say that those breeders have met together and have appointed a small committee, of whom Mr. Robert Miller is the chairman and this committee have the management of their affairs. All we do is to provide for the necessary examination of the certificates of pedigree. We have to supply them with house room for their woi'k when they are brought here, and supply the stationery.

Me do not want to be coerced into doing that which we do not believe to be contrary to the interests of our association.

I will explain that when my hon. friend sits down.
,, POSTER. That is the chief part of the information outside of the memorial which the hon. minister has.

speechtext: I -will explain to my hon. filend that his correspondent is mixing up two things that are entirely different. The
